entities.name: Conservation of Energy
entities.definition: Conservation of energy: for an isolated system the total energy — summed over all forms (kinetic, potential, thermal, chemical, nuclear, ...) — remains constant in time; energy transforms between forms but is neither created nor destroyed. Historical line: Mayer (1842), Joule (1843), Helmholtz (1847, 'Über die Erhaltung der Kraft'); standard statement per Halliday, Resnick, Walker 12th ed., Ch 8.

provenance.source: Halliday, Resnick, Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 12th ed., Ch 8 (potential energy and conservation of energy in isolated systems).

entities.name: Force
entities.definition: Force is the derived physical quantity of mechanical interaction: the net force on a body equals the time rate of change of its linear momentum, F = dp/dt (Newton, Principia Lex II); for constant mass this reduces to F = m a. Force is a vector quantity — it has magnitude and direction and adds by vector addition (net force = vector sum). SI derived unit: the newton, N = kg m s-2. Reference: Halliday, Resnick, Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 12th ed., Ch 5; Newton, Principia (1687), Lex II.

provenance.source: Halliday, Resnick, Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 12th ed., Ch 5: net force ΣF = m a; Principia (1687), Lex II: mutationem motus proportionalem esse vi motrici impressae.

entities.name: Kilogram
entities.definition: The kilogram (symbol: kg) is the SI base unit of mass. It is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the Planck constant h to be exactly 6.62607015e-34 when expressed in the unit joule second, J s, which is equal to kg m2 s-1, where the metre and the second are defined in terms of c and ΔνCs. Exact per BIPM definition of the kilogram (SI Brochure 9th ed., 2019, §2.3.1.2; the text of the 26th CGPM 2018, Resolution 1).

provenance.source: BIPM SI Brochure 9th ed. (2019) §2.3.1.2: the kilogram is defined by the fixed numerical value h = 6.62607015e-34 J s (kg m2 s-1), metre and second defined via c and ΔνCs.

entities.name: Length
entities.definition: Length is the SI base physical quantity of spatial extent — the measure of one-dimensional distance between two points in space. The metre is the unit in which length is expressed: 1 m = the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during 1/299,792,458 of a second (c fixed exact). Agreed per BIPM SI Brochure 9th ed. (2019), base quantities table; §2.3.1.

provenance.source: BIPM SI Brochure 9th ed. (2019): among the seven SI base quantities, length with base unit metre; metre defined by fixed numerical value of c in vacuum (2.3.1).

entities.name: Mass
entities.definition: Mass is the SI base physical quantity measuring a body's inertia and its quantity of matter. Its SI unit, the kilogram, is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the Planck constant h to be exactly 6.62607015e-34 when expressed in J s = kg m2 s-1, with the metre and second as separately defined (SI 2019 redefinition). Agreed per BIPM SI Brochure 9th ed. (2019) §2.3.1.

provenance.source: BIPM SI Brochure 9th ed. (2019): mass among the seven SI base quantities; kilogram defined by fixed h = 6.62607015e-34 kg m2 s-1 (2.3.1).

entities.name: Metre
entities.definition: The metre (symbol: m) is the base unit of length in the International System of Units (SI). It is scientifically defined as the length of the path travelled by light in a vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second. Exact: c=299,792,458 m/s. Agreed per BIPM SI Brochure 9th ed. 2019 redefinition, fixing c exact.

assumptions: role-unit-definition-fixed-constant (derived_from = the 2019 metre derives from the fixed c constant; dedicated value-claim relation reserved pending governance adoption)

provenance.source: BIPM SI Brochure 9th ed. (2019) §2.3.1, p130-132: The metre, symbol m, is the SI unit of length. It is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the speed of light in vacuum c to be 299792458 when expressed in m s-1. Exact: c=299,792,458 m/s. Agreed internationally.

entities.name: Newton's Second Law
entities.definition: Newton's second law of motion: the net external force on a system equals the time rate of change of its total linear momentum, ΣF = dp/dt; for constant mass this reduces to F = m a. Valid in classical (non-relativistic) mechanics in inertial reference frames. Stated by Isaac Newton as Lex II in Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica (1687); standard modern formulation per Halliday, Resnick, Walker 12th ed., Ch 5.

provenance.source: Halliday, Resnick, Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 12th ed., Ch 5 (Newton second law, force and momentum); Principia (1687), Lex II.

entities.name: Second
entities.definition: The second (symbol: s) is the SI base unit of time. It is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the caesium frequency ΔνCs, the unperturbed ground-state hyperfine transition frequency of the caesium-133 atom, to be exactly 9,192,631,770 when expressed in the unit hertz, which is equal to s-1. Exact per BIPM definition of the second (SI Brochure 9th ed., 2019, §2.3.1.1; the text of the 26th CGPM 2018, Resolution 1).

provenance.source: BIPM SI Brochure 9th ed. (2019) §2.3.1.1: the second is defined by the fixed numerical value of ΔνCs = 9,192,631,770 Hz (unperturbed hyperfine transition of Cs-133).

entities.name: Time
entities.definition: Time is the SI base physical quantity of duration and temporal sequence. Its SI unit, the second, is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the caesium frequency ΔνCs — the unperturbed ground-state hyperfine transition frequency of the caesium-133 atom — to be exactly 9,192,631,770 hertz (Hz = s-1): one second is the duration of 9,192,631,770 periods of the radiation corresponding to that transition. Exact per BIPM SI Brochure 9th ed. (2019) §2.3.1.

provenance.source: BIPM SI Brochure 9th ed. (2019): time among the seven SI base quantities; second defined by fixed ΔνCs = 9,192,631,770 Hz (2.3.1).
